Designated Crown Prince during his father's 1967 coronation, this dissident has lived in exile in the US since the 1979 revolution that abolished the monarchy his family once ruled — who is he?
Reza Pahlavi: Former Crown Prince of Iran (born 1960)
Valedictorian of Plains High School in Georgia, this American first lady became a lifelong champion of mental health and women's rights — who was she?
Rosalynn Carter: First Lady of the United States from 1977 to 1981.
Nominated by President George W. Bush in 2005, this jurist became just the second Italian American justice on the Supreme Court, after Antonin Scalia — who is he?
Samuel Alito: US Supreme Court justice since 2006.
Named after a 1968 Czechoslovak uprising, this brief South Korean democratization movement began the night President Park Chung Hee was assassinated in 1979 — what is it called?
Seoul Spring: Period of democratization in South Korea (1979–1980)

Led by the future Roman emperor Titus, an army encircled and breached the walls of this Jewish holy city, destroying the Second Temple after a bitter feud between rival factions cut off the population's own food supply — which historic event is this?
Siege of Jerusalem (70 CE): Part of the First Jewish–Roman War.
Wounded at Gallipoli before entering politics, this businessman led the Nationalist Party as the eighth prime minister of Australia from 1923 to 1929 — who was he?
Stanley Bruce: Prime Minister of Australia from 1923 to 1929. In office, Bruce pursued an energetic and diverse agenda.
He led the first government of Bangladesh as prime minister during the 1971 War of Independence and is seen as one of the most instrumental figures in the nation's birth — who was he?
Tajuddin Ahmad: Prime Minister of Bangladesh from 1971 to 1972.
This crime-busting New York governor famously prosecuted mobster "Lucky" Luciano, then lost the presidency twice — to FDR in 1944 and Truman in 1948 — who was he?
As chairman of Saudi Arabia's General Entertainment Authority, this Royal Court adviser also owned Spanish club Almería from 2019 to 2025 — who is he?
A free-love advocate and women's rights activist, she ran for president of the United States in 1872 — widely cited as the first woman to do so; who was she?
Victoria Woodhull: American women's suffrage activist (1838–1927)

Sparked by the 1791 Declaration of Pillnitz, this 1792–1797 conflict saw a loose alliance of European monarchies invade Revolutionary France, including the Duke of Brunswick's capture of Verdun — what was it called?
Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula
War of the First Coalition: 1792–1797 wars between France and European powers.
Born to mixed English-American parentage, this statesman led his nation through its darkest hour as Prime Minister during World War II. Who?
Winston Churchill: British statesman and writer (1874–1965)
This Central European nation emerged after World War I as a union of South Slavic peoples, survived until 1992, and was born from the merger of Serbia with a provisional state. What country was this?
Who among these was born first?
Patrick Geddes (born 1854) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four was born earliest?

Ivan Pavlov (born 1849) is the earliest of the four. Pavlov also conducted significant research on the physiology of digestion, for which he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1904.
Who among these was born first?
Benjamin Banneker (born 1731) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four came first?
Pascal (programming language) (founded 1970) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is an astronomer?
Aryabhata is an astronomer. The claim that Nalanda used to be located in Kusamapura/Pataliputra also cannot be proven.
Which of these is a mathematician?
Michael Atiyah is a mathematician. Sir Michael Francis Atiyah (22 April 1929 – 11 January 2019) was a British-Lebanese mathematician specialising in geometry.
What is the atomic number of Tin?
Tin is a chemical element; it has the symbol Sn (from Latin stannum) and atomic number 50.
What is the atomic number of Titanium?
Titanium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ti and atomic number 22.
In what year was Alexander Hamilton born?
Alexander Hamilton: Born out of wedlock in Charlestown on the Caribbean island of Nevis, Hamilton was orphaned as a child and taken in by a prosperous merchant.
In what year was Ivan Pavlov born?
Ivan Pavlov: Pavlov also conducted significant research on the physiology of digestion, for which he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1904.
In what year was Archimedes born?
Archimedes died during the siege of Syracuse, when he was killed by a Roman soldier despite orders that he should not be harmed.
In what year did Kalpana Chawla die?
Kalpana Chawla (July 1, 1962 – February 1, 2003) was an Indian-American astronaut and aerospace engineer who was the first woman of Indian origin to fly to space.
In what year did Rosalind Franklin die?
Rosalind Franklin: Rosalind Elsie Franklin (25 July 1920 – 16 April 1958) was an English chemist and X-ray crystallographer.
In what year was Oxycodone discovered?
Oxycodone: It is a highly addictive and commonly abused drug.
Mikoyan MiG-29: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. The Mikoyan MiG-29 (Russian: Микоян МиГ-29; NATO reporting name: Fulcrum) is a twin-engine fighter aircraft designed in the Soviet Union.
Which company manufactures BAE Systems Hawk?
BAE Systems Hawk: Hawker Siddeley. The BAE Systems Hawk is a British single-engine, subsonic, jet-powered advanced trainer aircraft.
Which country is Bombardier Challenger 600 series from?
Bombardier Challenger 600 series: Canada. At the end of 1975, Canadair began funding the development of LearStar 600, and then bought the design for a wide-cabin business jet in April 1976.
Who is credited with discovering Hassium?
GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
Hassium: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research. Hassium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Hs and atomic number 108.
Who is credited with discovering HD 209458 b?
HD 209458 b: Michel Mayor. It is sometimes informally called Osiris.
Who is credited with discovering Osmium?
Osmium: Smithson Tennant. Osmium (from Ancient Greek ὀσμή (osmḗ) 'smell') is a chemical element; it has symbol Os and atomic number 76.
This genus of succulent, spiky-leaved plants native to the arid Americas typically takes years to mature, with each rosette flowering only once before dying — what's the genus called?
Agave (Anglo-Hispanic) is a genus of monocots native to the arid regions of the Americas.
These mostly semiaquatic vertebrates are tetrapods that pointedly lack an amniotic membrane, splitting into just three living orders like the frogs and toads of Anura — what are they?
Amphibian are ectothermic, anamniotic, four-limbed vertebrate animals that constitute the class Amphibia.
Coined by a French naturalist in 1799 from a Tupi word for the sound macaws make, this genus name covers eight species of long-tailed, brightly plumed Neotropical parrots — which genus?
Ara (bird) is a Neotropical genus of macaws with eight extant species and at least two extinct species.
This fig species develops extra trunks from its own aerial prop roots, letting a single tree spread outward seemingly forever, one variety is even the national tree of India. Name it?
Banyan is a fig that develops accessory trunks from adjacent prop roots, allowing the tree to spread outwards indefinitely.

Found mainly in New Guinea, which family of forty-four species — the males famous for extravagant, elaborate plumage sprouting from their beaks, wings, tails, or heads — is confined largely to dense rainforest?
Bird-of-paradise are members of the family Paradisaeidae of the order Passeriformes.
This outdated 19th-century term for what's now called acute or chronic nephritis was marked by swelling and albumin showing up in the urine — what was it called?
Bright's disease is a historical classification of kidney diseases that are described in modern medicine as acute or chronic nephritis.
Bordered by Aquila, Sagittarius, and Aquarius in the sky's watery region, this half-goat, half-fish zodiac figure is the tiniest of the twelve — which constellation?
Capricornus is one of the constellations of the zodiac.
This genus of deciduous trees and shrubs in the beech family, native to the temperate Northern Hemisphere, gives its name to a widely eaten edible nut it produces — what's this tree (and nut) called?
Chestnut are the deciduous trees and shrubs in the genus Castanea, in the beech family Fagaceae.

Native to Australasia and ranging from the Philippines to the Solomon Islands, these 21 parrot species are recognizable by their prominent crests and curved bills, with plumage that's mostly white, grey, or black — name the group?
Cockatoo is any of the 21 species of parrots belonging to the family Cacatuidae, the only family in the superfamily Cacatuoidea, native to Australasia.

This family of fifteen tall, long-necked bird species mostly wears muted gray-and-white plumage with a patch of bare red skin on the face — except for one crowned genus that stands out — what bird is it?
Crane (bird) are a type of large bird with long legs and necks in the biological family Gruidae of the order Gruiformes.
When insulin runs short, the body burns fat into acidic ketones, causing deep gasping breaths and fruity-smelling breath in this potentially life-threatening emergency — what is it?
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a potentially life-threatening acute complication of diabetes mellitus.
Born in Dublin in 1869 into an old Anglo-Irish scientific family, she's considered the very first woman to work as a medical physicist — who was she?
Edith Anne Stoney (6 January 1869 - 25 June 1938) was an Irish physicist.

This Austrian physicist devised a foundational equation for calculating a quantum system's wave function and coined the term 'quantum entanglement,' sharing the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with Paul Dirac — who is he?
Erwin Schrödinger (12 August 1887 - 4 January 1961), sometimes written as Schroedinger or Schrodinger, was an Austrian theoretical physicist who developed fundamental results in quantum theory.
This body part is a prominent, usually flexible digit found on the forelimbs of most four-limbed vertebrates — on the hind limbs, the equivalent shorter digits are instead called toes. What is it?
Finger is a prominent digit on the forelimbs of most tetrapod vertebrate animals, especially those with prehensile extremities (i.e.

Cataloged by the astronomer Ptolemy in the second century AD and still one of the 88 modern constellations, this zodiac constellation takes its Latin name from the mythological twins Castor and Pollux — what's the constellation?
Gemini (constellation) is one of the constellations of the zodiac and is located in the northern celestial hemisphere.

This Russian mathematician resigned his research post in 2005 and later declared he'd quit the field entirely, disillusioned by its ethical standards, and now lives in seclusion in Saint Petersburg — who is he?
Grigori Perelman (born 13 June 1966) is a Russian mathematician and geometer who is known for his contributions to the fields of geometric analysis, Riemannian geometry, and geometric topology.
With a soft, uncalcified abdomen left dangerously exposed, this crustacean borrows empty snail shells to survive — over 800 species haul their homes around with them. What are they?
Hermit crab are anomuran decapod crustaceans of the superfamily Paguroidea that have adapted to occupy empty scavenged gastropod shells to protect their fragile abdomens.
A person with this condition is excessively and unduly worried about having a serious illness, alarmed by even the most minor symptom — what is it?

Hypochondriasis is a condition in which a person is excessively and unduly worried about having a serious illness. International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10) classifies hypochondriasis as a mental and behavioral disorder.

Native to the tropical Americas but now planted worldwide, this flowering plant genus of 49 species has one member so widely introduced it's considered an environmental weed on five continents — what genus is it?
Jacaranda is a genus of 49 species of flowering plants in the family Bignoniaceae, native to tropical and subtropical regions of the Americas while cultivated around the world.
Holding doctorates in both anthropology and medicine, this SS physician earned the grim nickname 'Angel of Death' for his experiments and selections at Auschwitz — who was he?

Josef Mengele (16 March 1911 - 7 February 1979), often dubbed the "Angel of Death", was a German military officer and physician during World War II at the Soviet front and then at Auschwitz during the Holocaust.
Home to aromatic herbs like mint, oregano, and lavender as well as the seed crop chia, this family of mostly herbaceous flowering plants is commonly known as the mints or deadnettles — which family?

Lamiaceae is a family of flowering plants commonly known as mints, deadnettles, or sages. The mint family as a whole has a cosmopolitan distribution comprising about 236 genera and around 6,900 to 7,200 species.
Named after a pioneer of sterile surgery, this genus of rod-shaped bacteria can multiply even at refrigerator temperatures and causes a rare but serious foodborne illness — what is it?
Listeria is a genus of bacteria that acts as an intracellular parasite in mammals.
Formed from two glucose units linked by an alpha(1→4) bond, which disaccharide, a reducing sugar unlike sucrose, is released when starch breaks down during malting?
Maltose (or), also known as maltobiose or malt sugar, is a disaccharide formed from two units of glucose joined with an (14) bond.
Nicknamed "quicksilver," this is the only metallic element that stays liquid at room temperature, and it's often mined as the red mineral cinnabar — which element is it?
Mercury (element) is a chemical element; it has symbol Hg and atomic number 80.
Classified by carbon count into trioses, pentoses, hexoses, and more, these colorless, water-soluble simple sugars are the basic building blocks of carbohydrates — what are they called?
Monosaccharide (from Greek monos: single, sacchar: sugar), also called simple sugars, are a class of organic compounds usually with the formula (CH2O)x.

Discovered in 1898 alongside krypton and xenon, this colorless noble gas is famous for the distinctive bright-red glow it emits, which led to its immediate identification as a new element — what gas, symbol Ne, is it?
Neon is a chemical element; it has the symbol Ne and the atomic number 10.
This English physicist identified electromagnetic radiation independently of Hertz, and named his improved early radio receiver the 'coherer' — whose key 'syntonic' tuning patents helped birth radio?
Oliver Lodge (12 June 1851 - 22 August 1940) was an English physicist and electrical engineer whose investigations into electromagnetic radiation (EMR) contributed to the development of radio.

Closely related to carrot and parsley, this pale, long-tapered root vegetable grows sweeter in flavor after winter frosts and produces yellow flowers if left unharvested into its second season — name the vegetable?
Parsnip (Pastinaca sativa) is a root vegetable closely related to carrot and parsley, all belonging to the flowering plant family Apiaceae.

Associated with the early 20th century, this philosophical movement tries to objectively describe subjective conscious experience exactly as it appears, without assuming anything about the outside world — which movement?
Phenomenology (philosophy) is a philosophical study and movement largely associated with the early 20th century that seeks to objectively investigate the nature of subjective, conscious experience.

It plays out everywhere from the clans of traditional societies up through modern governments, and its practitioners negotiate, make laws, and sometimes wage war; what is this activity of settling a society's affairs?
Politics is the activity of settling affairs in an organized society. Politics is usually concerned with resolving issues within a society via a government.
This Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacterium selectively blocks antibiotics from crossing its outer membrane, making it a notorious cause of hospital-acquired pneumonia — what is it?
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a common encapsulated, Gram-negative, aerobic-facultatively anaerobic, rod-shaped bacterium that can cause disease in plants and animals, including humans.
What fat-soluble alcohol form of vitamin A — found in fish, dairy, and meat — is essential for vision, skin maintenance, and immune function, and is used as a supplement to prevent xerophthalmia?
Retinol is a hydrolytic metabolite of retinyl esters belonging to the group of vitamin A1 as an alcohol form.

These lizard-like amphibians, grouped in the order Urodela, keep a tail throughout both their larval and adult life stages — unlike their tailless amphibian cousins the frogs and toads. What animal is it?

Salamander are a group of amphibians typically characterized by their lizard-like appearance, with slender bodies, blunt snouts, short limbs projecting at right angles to the body, and the presence of a tail in both larvae and adults.

Essentially plasma with the clotting factors and cells removed, this pale yellow fluid still carries antibodies, hormones, and electrolytes and is central to typing tests done before a transfusion — what is it?
Serum (blood) is the fluid and solvent component of blood which does not play a role in clotting.

This genus of about 60 evergreen flowering plant species, native to the tropical Americas and Southeast Asia, is commonly grown as a houseplant valued for its large leaves and elegant white blooms — what genus is it?
Spathiphyllum is a genus of about 60 species of monocotyledonous flowering plants in the family Araceae, native to tropical regions of the Americas and southeastern Asia.
Educated in Rotterdam through World War II, this Indonesian economist later served as minister of finance, trade, and research under two different presidents — who was he?
Sumitro Djojohadikusumo (27 May 1917 - 9 March 2001) was an Indonesian statesman and one of the country's most influential economists.
Enhanced by painted scenery and stagecraft like lighting, this live performing art shares its name with the very buildings where its shows are staged — what is it?

Theatre is a collaborative form of performing art that uses live performers, usually actors, to present experiences of a real or imagined event before a live audience in a specific place, often a stage.
Latin for 'three-headed,' this large muscle on the back of the upper arm has three parts, one of which also crosses the shoulder joint — name the muscle?
Triceps (Latin for "three-headed muscle of the arm"), is a large muscle on the back of the upper limb of many vertebrates.
First glimpsed in 1892 through tobacco-plant disease and counted as the most numerous biological entity on Earth, this submicroscopic agent can only replicate inside a living cell. What is it?
Virus is a submicroscopic infectious agent that replicates only inside the living cells of an organism.

This unit of time is based on how long Earth takes to complete one full orbit around the Sun, with the precise scientific definition running about 365 days, 5 hours, and 48 minutes — what unit is this?

Year is a unit of time based on how long it takes the Earth to orbit the Sun. In scientific use, the tropical year (approximately 365 solar days, 5 hours, 48 minutes, 45 seconds) and the sidereal year (about 20 minutes longer) are more exact.
Also called sweet flag, this wetland plant contains psychoactive compounds and has been banned from American food products despite centuries of use in traditional medicine — which species?
Acorus calamus: Species of plant. Acorus calamus (also called sweet flag, sway or muskrat root, among many other common names) is a species of flowering plant with psychoactive chemicals.
This congenital condition causes a total or partial absence of pigment, leading to white hair, pale skin, and often pink or reddish eyes — what is it called?
Albinism: Disorder causing lack of pigmentation.
Native to North America but now invasive across Europe after being introduced, this semiaquatic mustelid preys on rodents, fish, and frogs — which animal?
American mink: Semiaquatic species of mustelid. Because of range expansion, the American mink is classed as a least-concern species by the IUCN.
Nicknamed "the heart of the scorpion," this reddish supergiant is the brightest star in its constellation — what is it?
Antares: Binary star in the constellation Scorpius.
Sold under the brand name Abilify, this atypical antipsychotic treats schizophrenia, bipolar mania, and irritability linked to autism spectrum disorder — what is it?
Aripiprazole: Atypical antipsychotic medication. Aripiprazole is taken by mouth or via injection into a muscle.
Native to the Americas and prized for thousands of years for its unusually oily fruit, this evergreen of the laurel family bears what's botanically a giant berry around a single seed — what is it?
Avocado: Species of flowering plant in the laurel family.
Sometimes called the common, lawn, or English variety, this European plant is considered the archetypal member of the daisy family — what's its scientific name?

Bellis perennis: Species of plant in the daisy family. Bellis perennis ( BEL-iss pə-REN-iss), the daisy, is a European species of the family Asteraceae, often considered the archetypal species of the name daisy.
This medical term for blood escaping the circulatory system describes a healthy person as able to lose 10 to 15 percent of their total volume without serious harm — what is it called?
Bleeding: Blood escaping from the circulatory system. Bleeding, hemorrhage, haemorrhage or blood loss, is blood escaping from the circulatory system from damaged blood vessels.
Making up just 2.6 percent of the brain's weight, this stalk-like structure connects the cerebrum to the spinal cord and houses all ten pairs of cranial nerve origins — what is it?
Brainstem: Posterior part of the brain, adjoining and structurally continuous.
Its Latin name means "chisel-bearing," a nod to the stout egg-laying organs of its members — which insect suborder includes grasshoppers, ground-hoppers, and pygmy mole crickets?
Caelifera: Suborder of insects. The latter should not be confused with the mole crickets (Gryllotalpidae), which belong to the other Orthopteran suborder Ensifera.
A founder of humanistic psychology, this American psychologist pioneered person-centered therapy, an approach that also shaped student-centered learning in education — who is he?
Certified in 1984 and developed into a freighter variant for FedEx, this single-engine turboprop utility plane typically seats nine and can be fitted with floats or skis — which aircraft?
Cessna 208 Caravan: Family of utility transport aircraft.
Blooming in autumn and closely associated with the month of November, this East Asian flowering genus in the daisy family boasts thousands of horticultural varieties — which flower?
Chrysanthemum: Genus of flowering plants in the daisy family.

Triggered by an abnormal immune response to gluten found in wheat, barley, and rye, this chronic autoimmune condition mainly affects the small intestine and often causes malabsorption in children — which condition?
Coeliac disease: Autoimmune disorder. Coeliac disease (Commonwealth English) or celiac disease (American English) is a chronic autoimmune disease, mainly affecting the small intestine.
Also known as the Cornelian cherry, this dogwood-family shrub or small tree is native to western and southern Europe as well as southwestern Asia — what's its scientific name?
Cornus mas: Species of flowering plant in the family Cornaceae.
Also called Bermuda grass, this hardy warm-climate turf species is ironically not native to the island of the same name — which plant, by its scientific name?
Cynodon dactylon: Species of grass. Cynodon dactylon, commonly known as Bermuda grass or as couch grass in Australia and New Zealand, is a grass found worldwide in warm and tropical climates.
This central nervous system stimulant is the 'right-handed' mirror-image form of a well-known molecule, prescribed for ADHD and narcolepsy and sometimes given as an inactive prodrug — what is it?
Dextroamphetamine: CNS stimulant and isomer of amphetamine.
A broad-spectrum member of the tetracycline class, this antibiotic treats everything from acne and chlamydia to Lyme disease and cholera — though it'll make you sunburn more easily. Which drug?
Doxycycline: Tetracycline-class antibiotic. It is used to treat bacterial pneumonia, acne, chlamydia infections, Lyme disease, cholera, typhus, and syphilis, and is sometimes used to prevent malaria.
Despite its name, this South American freshwater fish is actually a knifefish, not a true eel, and produces powerful discharges using specialized tissue — which species?
Electrophorus electricus: South American electric fish. It is considered as a freshwater teleost which contains an electrogenic tissue that produces electric discharges.
This flowering shrub in the family Erythroxylaceae is one of only two species whose leaves are cultivated to produce a notorious stimulant — which plant is it?
Erythroxylum coca: Species of flowering plant.
Sporting an orange-red breast rimmed in grey and brown upperparts, this small insect-eating songbird ranges from Western Siberia to North Africa — which bird?
European robin: Species of bird. It is found across Europe, as far east as Western Siberia, and as far south as North Africa.
Belonging to the genus Abies, these evergreen conifers have cones that stand upright like candles and disintegrate at maturity, and some varieties serve as Christmas trees — which conifer genus?
Fir: Genus of coniferous trees. The genus is most closely related to Keteleeria, a small genus confined to eastern Asia.
The largest region of the brain's cerebral hemispheres, this most-forward area contains the primary motor cortex and is separated from the parietal and temporal regions by two grooves — what is it?
Frontal lobe: Part of the brain. The most anterior ventral, orbital end of the frontal lobe is known as the frontal pole, which is one of the three so-called poles of the cerebrum.
First described by J. D. Hooker in 1889 and nicknamed the Transvaal or Barberton daisy for its South African origins, what genus of flowering plant is this?
Gerbera: Genus of plants. Gerbera ( JUR-bər-ə or GUR-bər-ə) L. is a genus of plants in the Asteraceae (Compositae) family.
This cluster of immune cells forms around bacteria, fungi, or foreign material the body can't otherwise clear away — what is it called?
Granuloma: Inflammatory aggregation of immune cells.

This British aviation entrepreneur held three Guinness World Records after visiting the South Pole, the Challenger Deep, and space, then died in 2023 aboard the submersible that imploded near the Titanic wreck — who was he?
Using only a triangle's three side lengths and their semiperimeter, this ancient geometric method computes the triangle's area — what is it known as?
Heron's formula: Triangle area in terms of side lengths.
Generally colourless, hydrophobic, and faintly gasoline-scented, which organic compound is made entirely of hydrogen and carbon and includes everything from methane to paraffin wax?

Hydrocarbon: Organic compound consisting entirely of hydrogen and carbon. In the fossil fuel industries, hydrocarbon refers to naturally occurring petroleum, natural gas and coal, or their hydrocarbon derivatives and purified forms.
Designed in 1967 to replace the An-12 and haul heavy machinery into remote, poorly served regions, this four-engine Soviet airlifter earned the NATO name 'Candid' — what is it?
Ilyushin Il-76: Russian heavy four-engined military transport jet aircraft.
The biggest cat in the Americas, it has a bite so powerful it can crack a turtle's shell or punch straight through a skull between the ears — which animal?
Jaguar: Large cat native to the Americas.
Trained originally in mathematics at Cambridge, this English economist's Depression-era writings became the foundation for a whole school of macroeconomic thought bearing his name — who is he?
This classical physics model imagines matter as countless invisible particles in constant, random collisions, explaining pressure, temperature and viscosity alike — what is it?
Kinetic theory of gases: Understanding of gas properties in terms of molecular motion.
Weighing up to 1,100 pounds, this heaviest of all non-crocodilian reptiles lacks a bony shell, its carapace covered instead in oily, leather-like flesh — what animal is it?
Leatherback sea turtle: Species of marine reptile.
Defined as exactly one cubic decimetre and rooted in an old French unit called the litron, what metric measure of volume is this?
Litre: Unit of volume. The litre (Commonwealth spelling) or liter (American spelling) (SI symbols L and l, other symbol used: ℓ) is a metric unit of volume.
A Russian linguist by training, this woman served two separate terms as first lady of Russia, from 2000 to 2008 and again from 2012 to 2014 — who is she?
Lyudmila Putina: Ex-wife of Vladimir Putin (born 1958)
Prized for its sweet, pine-and-citrus flavor, this perennial herb is often considered synonymous with oregano in parts of the Middle East — what is it?
Marjoram: Perennial herb. It is also called pot marjoram, although this name is also used for other cultivated species of Origanum.
Also nicknamed 'Cornish salmon,' this predatory fish is often netted alongside the Atlantic herring it preys on, and is heavily overfished across European waters — which fish?
Merluccius merluccius: Species of fish. Merluccius merluccius or the European hake is a merluccid hake of the genus Merluccius.

Codenamed 'Havoc' by NATO, this Soviet tandem-seat attack helicopter carries a single gun in an under-nose barbette and, unlike its predecessor, has no secondary troop-transport role. What aircraft is this?
Mil Mi-28: Russian attack helicopter. The Mil Mi-28 (NATO reporting name "Havoc") is a Soviet heavy-weight, all-weather, day-night, tandem-seat anti-armour military attack helicopter.
Its wings make an odd whistling sound on take-off, and one pair may raise up to six broods a year — which abundant North American gamebird?
Mourning dove: North American bird in the family Columbidae.
Descended from Southern Italy's traditional guard dogs and closely related to the Cane Corso, this large wrinkly Italian breed was recognized in 1949 — which dog breed?
Neapolitan Mastiff: Italian breed of dog. The Neapolitan Mastiff or Mastino Napoletano is an Italian breed of large dog of mastiff type.

Flown by William J. Knight to a record 4,520 mph in 1967 — a mark that still stands — this rocket-powered aircraft was part of an experimental series operated by the Air Force and NASA — which aircraft?
North American X-15: Rocket-powered aircraft and spaceplane operated by the US Air Force and NASA.
The most arboreal of the great apes, with long arms, short legs and reddish-brown hair, this genus Pongo primate survives today only in the rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra — what is it?
Orangutan: Genus of Asian apes. The most arboreal of the great apes, orangutans spend most of their time in trees.
Commonly known as the bullet ant for its notoriously painful sting, which insect species inhabits the humid lowland rainforests of Central and South America?
This serous membrane lines the abdominal cavity and serves as a conduit for the blood vessels and nerves of the organs it covers — what is it called?
Peritoneum: Membrane that forms lining of abdominal cavity or coelom.
This French physicist shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with his wife, making them the first married couple to win a Nobel — who is he?
Pierre Curie: French physicist and chemist (1859–1906)
Also called quaking aspen for the way its leaves flutter in the slightest breeze, which poplar species is native to the Old World's cool temperate regions?
This evergreen shrub or small tree native to South America is pollinated chiefly by the honey bee and gives us a popular tropical fruit — what species is it?
Psidium guajava: Species of flowering plant.
Born from refraction, internal reflection, and dispersion of light in water droplets, this arc always appears in the patch of sky directly opposite the sun — what is it?
Made of a large and small subunit built from RNA and protein, which cellular structure translates messenger RNA into chains of amino acids?
Ribosome: Macromolecular machine that synthesizes proteins in cells.

Built by a Swedish manufacturer, this single-engine fighter was the first mass-produced canard-design aircraft and the first with a digital avionics computer, unsurpassed until the Tornado arrived in 1981 — which jet?
Saab 37 Viggen: 1967 Swedish fighter aircraft family.
Native to cold-temperate Eurasia, this spiny deciduous shrub yields a fruit and oil prized in both cooking and cosmetics — what plant is it?
Sea buckthorn: Species of flowering plant in the family Elaeagnaceae.
Sitting just below carbon in group 14 of the periodic table, this blue-grey, brittle semiconductor is essential to plants and dominates the world's transistors and solar cells — which element is it?
Silicon: Chemical element with atomic number 14 (Si)
Commonly grown as an easy-care houseplant that tolerates low light, this genus of about 60 tropical species is better known by the nickname 'peace lily' — what genus is it?
Spathiphyllum: Genus of plants. Certain species of Spathiphyllum are commonly known as spath or peace lilies.
Usually found in pairs and recognized as a leading cause of pneumonia since the late 19th century, which bacterium often lives harmlessly in the respiratory tracts of healthy carriers?

Founder and chairman of the world's largest express transportation company, this American business magnate stepped down as CEO in 2022 after building a $5.3 billion fortune — who is he?
Frederick W. Smith: American business magnate (1944–2025)
Acquired by Chrysler from American Motors in 1987, this SUV-focused automobile brand's 1963 Wagoneer is credited with starting the luxury SUV segment — which brand?
Jeep: American automobile brand. Jeep is an American automobile brand, now owned by multi-national corporation Stellantis.
Born in 1924 from a merger of three picture companies, this Culver City studio boasted "more stars than there are in heaven" and is now owned by Amazon — which studio is it?
Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer: American film and distribution company.

Founded in 1997 by Hiroshi Mikitani, this Tokyo-based tech conglomerate has been dubbed 'the Amazon of Japan' for its sprawling online marketplace, fintech arm, and telecom business — what company is it?
Rakuten: Japanese e-commerce and technology company.
Formed in 2021 by merging France's PSA Group with Fiat Chrysler, this carmaker sells under 14 brands including Jeep, Maserati, Peugeot and Ram — what is it?
Stellantis: Multinational automotive car manufacturing corporation.
One of America's 'Big Four' banks, this company's main office in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, makes it a legal 'citizen' of that state in most federal courts — which bank is this?
Wells Fargo: American multinational banking and financial services company.
